item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q010_rossmann_family_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places all three groups in the alpha/beta class c, Rossmann fold c.2, and NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily c.2.1, but in distinct families. Thus alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains, CoA-binding domains, and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains are treated as probable remote homologs sharing an ancestral Rossmann-like nucleotide-binding core—not as closely related proteins with interchangeable functions. The family separation records substantial functional divergence: alcohol-dehydrogenase-like domains participate in oxidoreductase systems, CoA-binding domains recognize coenzyme A in their own enzymatic contexts, and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains occur in channel-regulatory machinery. Neither a shared fold nor even superfamily membership justifies transferring substrate specificity, catalytic activity, channel function, ligand preference, oligomeric state, or interaction partners. For modeling, a c.2.1 member may supply a template for the conserved core, but loops, active-site residues, insertions, interfaces, and multidomain context can differ; representatives should therefore be chosen first from the same family and, ideally, with matching ligand and architecture rather than merely from the same superfamily. Any functional assignment should be corroborated with sequence-profile evidence, detailed structural alignment, conservation of ligand/catalytic residues, domain context, and biochemical or binding data.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
